cards.title: Build a 48-month subscription financial model from ad spend down
cards.summary: Excel layout for forecasting a DTC subscription business: assumptions tab in blue, customer acquisition tab driving orders, then a monthly P&L out to 48 months.
cards.use_when: You need to plan store operations, model a raise, or test whether your ad budget and churn can produce a profitable subscription business before committing spend.
steps: Set a 48-month timeline (M1–M48) across the top; freeze panes so the active cell keeps time labels visible as you scroll right.
Colour-code inputs: hard-coded assumptions in dark blue, all formulas in black, so anyone editing the file knows which numbers they may change and which are calculated.
On an acquisition tab, start with monthly advertising spend (e.g. $5,000 ramping to $15,000 by month 7, then growing ~7.5%/month) and a paid CAC assumption.
Compute new customers = ad spend / paid CAC for each month. Model CAC improving over year 1 (e.g. $35 down to $20) as organic and email list growth lower blended acquisition cost.
Apply a monthly churn rate (the example uses a flat 15%) to recurring customers: retained = prior total customers x (1 - churn), so total orders = new + recurring.
Build the P&L from these order volumes: gross revenue = AOV x orders; subtract discounts and refunds (both applied only to new-order revenue) to get net revenue.
Feed COGS (product, packaging, fulfillment, customer service, merchant fees) and opex (personnel, advertising, other marketing, tech, an unallocated 'unknown' bucket) to land on operating income.
Add a roll-up summary tab that sums each quarter across years, plus starting cash and cash balance, to calculate runway in months.
caveats: All figures (CAC, churn, AOV, cost percentages) are illustrative assumptions, not benchmarks; replace them with your own data.
A flat churn rate is a simplification — real cohorts often churn differently in early vs later months.
The model is a planning sandbox; it does not predict actual performance.

cards.title: Discounts vs CAC: when a discount is mathematically neutral
cards.summary: If a discount lifts conversion enough that CAC falls by the same dollar amount, post-marketing per-order contribution margin is unchanged — so discounting is a CAC substitute, not automatically a margin loss.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a discount or promo on a PDP, landing page or email flow, and whether the discount is actually cheaper than buying the same customers through paid ads.
steps: Work out your current paid CAC per new customer (total paid marketing / new customer orders).
Estimate how much the discount lifts first-order conversion, and translate that lift into the implied reduction in cost per acquired customer — a discount effectively subsidises acquisition.
Compare the discount's dollar cost per incremental new order against the CAC you would otherwise pay for that order.

If the discount reduces effective acquisition cost by roughly the same dollar amount it gives away, the post-marketing contribution per order is identical — choose on the basis of which produces the volume and quality of customers you want.

When discounting deeply, attach the discount explicitly to an on-ramp into a loyalty or subscription program so the acquired customer has a path to recurring contribution rather than being a one-off transaction.
Model several discount scenarios in your financial model and pick the one that maximises total company profit at your fixed ad budget, not the one with the highest conversion.
caveats: The neutrality claim only holds when the discount changes acquisition cost by the same dollar amount; larger discounts still reduce margin.
The source explicitly warns against using deep discounts for standard one-off flash sales — they should be tied to a loyalty/subscription on-ramp.
Conversion lift estimates are assumptions until tested.

cards.title: Split COGS into product and fulfillment to read ecommerce margins
cards.summary: Separate product cost from fulfillment cost instead of lumping them into one COGS line, so you can see product gross profit and fulfillment drag independently.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly store P&L, diagnosing why margins moved, or deciding whether a shipping, pick-and-pack or packaging decision is eroding profitability.
steps: On your income statement, split COGS into (a) product cost (materials, manufacturing) and (b) fulfillment (shipping, pick and pack, packaging, other delivery charges).
Calculate product gross profit = revenue - product COGS, and express it as a percentage of revenue (the example shows roughly 73% converting to product gross profit).
Calculate contribution margin = revenue - product COGS - fulfillment. This is what remains to fund marketing, payroll and other opex.

Divide each individual fulfillment line by revenue month by month to pinpoint which charge is moving — the example shows pick-and-pack and packaging holding roughly stable while shipping and other charges crept up.
Track these percentages over several months; stable product and fulfillment percentages indicate predictable margins, while a swing in one line tells you where to intervene.
Use contribution margin per order (total contribution margin / total orders) as the number to compare against cost per new order.
caveats: Splitting COGS this way is the presenter's preference for ecommerce analysis; accountants will usually report a single COGS line.
Percentage shifts can reflect product mix change rather than true cost inflation.

cards.title: Read a monthly P&L as percent of revenue to spot trajectory and margin drift
cards.summary: Lay revenue down through product cost, fulfillment, marketing and opex as percentages of revenue to see growth, margin predictability and where profitability broke.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly store review: assessing whether the business is growing, whether margins are stable, and which line caused a profitable month to turn into a loss.
steps: Present the period side by side with a percent-of-revenue column next to every dollar line.
Order the lines: revenue, product COGS, product gross profit, fulfillment, contribution margin, marketing, post-marketing contribution, opex, operating income.
Check trajectory first: is revenue increasing month over month and are margins predictable or drifting?
Compare contribution margin % across months — stable percentages (e.g. ~42–43%) mean cost structure is under control.
Watch marketing as a percentage of revenue: it will bounce around when scaling, and a jump (e.g. 29% to 39%) can be the single cause of a loss month even when contribution margin held.
Trace the loss to a line before reacting — in the example, an August marketing spike pushed operating income from +7.5% to -2.2% and back to +6.4%.
Aim for break-even or better on the first order, since ecommerce repeat behaviour is generally limited; only exceptional stores are strongly profitable on the first order after marketing.
caveats: Saying ecommerce has 'generally' limited repeat behaviour is the presenter's generalisation; repeat-heavy categories exist.
Percentages can mask absolute-scale changes; read both.

cards.title: Compute per-order unit economics: AOV, product cost, fulfillment, contribution
cards.summary: Divide each P&L line by total orders to get AOV, product cost per order, fulfillment per order and contribution margin per order.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether each order is actually profitable before marketing, and comparing month-to-month stability of your order-level economics.
steps: AOV = total revenue / total orders (example: $232).
Product COGS per order = total product COGS / total orders (example: $62).
Fulfillment per order = total fulfillment / total orders (example: $71).
Contribution margin per order = AOV - product cost per order - fulfillment per order (example: $99).
Drag the formulas across months to see whether per-order economics are consistent; in the example contribution margin per order stayed stable even as revenue grew.

For noisy months, compute a trailing average: total revenue / total orders, total product COGS / total orders, total fulfillment / total orders across the whole period (example: $238 AOV, $64 product, $74 fulfillment, ~$100 contribution).
Keep customer counts, order counts and unit counts distinct — orders exceed customers, and units exceed orders when baskets average more than one item.
caveats: Blended per-order figures hide product-mix differences and seasonality.
AOV varies by promotion and channel; a trailing average may hide a recent shift.

cards.title: Add per-unit product economics to find your most profitable SKU
cards.summary: Calculate revenue, product gross profit and contribution margin per unit for each top SKU, because blended per-order numbers hide product-mix differences.
cards.use_when: Product selection, pricing and merchandising decisions — deciding which SKUs to push, bundle or drop based on margin per unit rather than revenue share alone.
steps: Pull a report that isolates sales by product; the summary financials report will not give you this.
For each top SKU, calculate average revenue per unit, product gross profit per unit and contribution margin per unit.

Compare both absolute dollars and percentages of revenue. Example: Product A (60% of sales) earns $230 revenue, $163 product profit (71% of revenue) and $92 contribution (40% of revenue); Product B (25% of sales) earns $122 revenue, $104 product profit (86% of revenue) and $74 contribution (61% of revenue).

Note the tension: Product A is more profitable per unit in dollars, Product B is more profitable as a percentage of revenue — the right choice depends on whether you optimise for cash per order or margin rate.
Compare per-unit contribution to the blended contribution margin per order: in the example the average order has higher contribution than either product alone, because customers buy multiple units.
Use the result to decide which SKUs to feature on the PDP, which to bundle together, and where a small markup is defensible.
caveats: Per-unit data requires a separate report; a channel- or order-level report will not produce it.
Higher margin-rate products can still be worse if their lower absolute contribution does not cover acquisition cost.

cards.title: Calculate blended CAC from total marketing and new customer orders
cards.summary: CAC/CPA is total marketing spend divided by new customer orders only — returning orders are excluded because they carry little paid marketing cost.
cards.use_when: Setting or auditing acquisition budgets, and comparing what you pay per new customer against the contribution margin that customer produces.
steps: Pull total new customer orders for the period and total marketing spend for the same period; do not include returning customer orders in the denominator.
Blended CAC = total marketing / total new customer orders (the example shows $74, $113, $100 across three months, $97 blended).
Compare blended CAC against contribution margin per new order: in the example, only the month where marketing cost per new order exceeded contribution margin per order was also the loss month.

To go beyond a blended figure, build the funnel by channel and stage — top-of-funnel exposure and nurturing activities (content), then conversion activities (deals, discounts) — to calculate channel-level CAC for Facebook, Google and other sources.
Use channel-level CAC to shift budget toward the sources whose CAC sits comfortably below contribution margin, and investigate the ones that do not.
caveats: Blended CAC mixes channels and is only directionally correct; channel CAC requires funnel-level tracking.
A single month's CAC can be distorted by campaign timing and seasonality; the source suggests trailing averages for noisy data.

cards.title: Build customer retention cohorts to measure true repeat purchase behaviour
cards.summary: Group customers by first purchase month and track their orders over subsequent months to see real lifetime purchase frequency, not just first-month averages.
cards.use_when: Forecasting LTV, judging whether a subscription or replenishment offer is working, or deciding whether retention spend is justified by actual repeat behaviour.
steps: Define cohorts by the month of a customer's first purchase; anyone repurchasing later stays in their original cohort (e.g. March = 167 first-time customers, April = 436, May = 659).
For each cohort, record orders in each subsequent month of lifetime (M2, M3, M4...), reading the grid diagonally to reconstruct total orders in a given calendar month.

Compute orders per customer over the observed window: the March cohort's 167 customers placed 330 orders in six months, about 1.98 orders each — nearly double the ~1.2 orders a customer appears to place in their first month.

To reconstruct a month's total orders, add that month's new customer orders to the diagonal of prior cohorts' later-lifetime orders (e.g. June new + May's M2 + April's M3 + March's M4 = recurring orders).
Use cohort order counts, not raw averages of all customers, to estimate LTV and to check whether CAC is recovered over the customer's real lifetime.
caveats: Cohorts require large data sets and a long enough history to read later months.
Early months of a cohort are incomplete; do not read M6 counts as that cohort's final behaviour.

cards.title: Define LTV as lifetime contribution margin and test it against CAC
cards.summary: Customer lifetime value is the total contribution margin a customer generates across their whole relationship — compare it to the marketing investment that acquired them to see if the model is profitable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale ad spend, raise prices, launch a subscription, or accept a slower payback in exchange for profitable scale.
steps: Define LTV as cumulative contribution margin (revenue minus product cost minus fulfillment) across all a customer's purchases, not as revenue.
Derive it from retention cohorts rather than blended averages — the source is explicit that cohorts tell a more exact story.
Compare LTV against CAC per new customer, and also check whether individual orders cover their own marketing cost, since ecommerce generally shows limited repeat behaviour.
If first-order contribution margin is below CAC, the business depends on repeat purchases to become profitable — validate that assumption with cohort data before scaling spend.
Use the split between first-order economics and lifetime economics to decide whether to push for break-even on the first order or accept a payback period across later orders.
caveats: LTV built on incomplete cohorts will overstate or understate the truth depending on maturity.
The recommendation to be break-even or better on every order is the presenter's stated preference, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Simplify a startup payroll model with salary x headcount ÷ 12
cards.summary: Forecast personnel cost from role salaries and headcount assumptions, plus a benefits load, instead of building a named-employee payroll.
cards.use_when: Building or updating the opex section of a startup or store financial model where you need a defensible payroll line without individual offer letters.
steps: List roles (marketing/sales, merchandising, product, technology, executive/admin) with an average annual salary per role.
Add benefits as a percentage of payroll — the example uses 25% in the US for healthcare, payroll taxes and 401k matching.
For each month and role, calculate salary / 12 x number of people in that role; lock the salary cell with F4 (absolute reference) so the formula copies across all 48 columns.
Lay out headcount as a separate grid of numbers per role per month, so hiring plans (e.g. add one person when revenue hits a milestone, then hold) are explicit and editable.
Sum all role salaries, multiply by the benefits percentage, and show total personnel as its own bold line.
Make the hiring plan narratively logical — the point of the model is that an investor can read it and see a plan for spending a round sensibly, not too fast.
caveats: Average salary per role is a simplification; real payroll varies by seniority and location.
The 25% benefits load is a US-specific example assumption.

cards.title: Include an unallocated 'unknown' opex bucket
cards.summary: Reserve a percentage of revenue in the model for expenses you cannot yet name, so the forecast does not understate cash burn.
cards.use_when: Building the opex section of a store financial model or budget, especially pre-launch or when scaling into new channels with uncertain costs.
steps: Create an 'other opex' category calculated as a fixed percentage of revenue (the example uses 10% of revenue in perpetuity).
Treat it as a deliberate catch-all for known-unknowns — tooling, agency retainers, contractors, one-off costs you have not scoped.
Keep it separate from the identified lines (advertising, other marketing such as PR or Facebook consultants, technology/hardware/software) so you can still see and edit those individually.
When actuals arrive, move spend out of the unknown bucket into named categories rather than letting it grow silently.
caveats: The 10% figure is an illustrative assumption in the source model, not a benchmark.
A catch-all can mask poor cost discipline if it is never reviewed against actuals.

cards.title: Set up a quarterly roll-up with starting cash to calculate runway
cards.summary: A summary tab that sums quarters and years across a starting cash balance shows how long the business can operate before it needs more funding.
cards.use_when: Founder or investor reporting: answering how far a raised amount stretches, when cash turns negative, and which year the business becomes profitable.
steps: Create a roll-up tab that only sums cells from the monthly model — do not recalculate anything there.
Lay quarters across the top (Q1–Q4 with a full-year total) and years down the side.
Include the key lines only: gross revenue, net revenue, COGS, gross profit, gross margin %, advertising, merchandising, personnel, other opex, total opex, operating income.
Add starting cash (the amount raised) and calculate each period's cash balance as opening balance plus the period's loss or profit.
Calculate runway as the number of periods until the cash balance turns negative — in the example, $3M with those assumptions lasted about two years, going negative early in year 3.
Sanity-check the roll-up against the monthly model: summing the last 12 months of operating profit in both should match (the example checks $508,419).
caveats: Runway is only as good as the underlying assumptions; the source stresses that actuals will differ.
Fundraising takes time, so the source advises knowing the runway well in advance and starting the raise early.

cards.title: Format a financial model for fast reading: colours, brackets, freeze panes
cards.summary: Use consistent colour conventions, accounting format with zero-suppression, and freeze panes so a large model stays readable and auditable.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any store P&L or financial model that others will read or edit.
steps: Apply the convention: dark blue = hard-coded input, black = formula, so editors instantly see what is safe to change.
Put a top and double-bottom border around the most important lines — revenue, gross profit, operating profit — so the eye lands on them in a dense sheet.
Use accounting format on key totals and suppress zeros so the model stays clean without noise.
Freeze panes so time headers and category labels remain visible while scrolling in both directions.
Build models without the mouse where possible (absolute cell references, border shortcuts via the keyboard) — the source says this pays back as models grow large.
Format with restraint: the source notes some people waste time over-formatting, but a little is worth doing.
caveats: Formatting conventions only help if everyone editing the file follows them.
The colour convention is a modelling norm, not a technical requirement.

cards.title: Build a standard VC-style 4-year model — and know its limits
cards.summary: Venture investors typically want about four years of monthly projections; the source demonstrates a 48-month model from a $3M raise for a coffee subscription.
cards.use_when: Preparing a data room or investor conversation, or stress-testing whether your store's plan supports the growth story a raise implies.
steps: Extend the monthly model to 48 months (four years) and keep the assumptions on a separate, colour-coded tab.
Drive the whole model from a handful of core inputs: advertising spend, paid CAC, churn, AOV, discount and refund rates, and cost percentages.
Show the trajectory explicitly in the roll-up: rising gross margin, revenue growth, and the year of maximum loss versus the year the business reaches operating profit.
Use the model to test improvements — the source suggests checking whether better packaging or product-cost percentages move your break-even month earlier.
In the worked example, the business first turns profitable around month 45; that is a property of those assumptions, not a general rule.
Present both the premise and the fragility: this model is only as credible as the assumptions inside it, so be ready to defend each one.
caveats: A four-year horizon is the VC convention shown here, not a universal forecasting rule.
The example's break-even month and $1.9M monthly revenue at month 48 are outputs of the sample assumptions, not targets.
The source's own caveat: the model exists to test whether the idea can make money at all.
